blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Write a comparison that keeps both texts in view in every paragraph.

blocks.heading: The comparative paragraph
blocks.text: A strong comparative paragraph holds both texts in every sentence: a point about one, the paired evidence from the other, and the explanation by purpose, audience or context. "My response opens with direct address — ‘Good morning’ — whereas the source opens with a headline, because a speech must find its hall before it can make its case, while an article must find its reader." Three moves in one sentence, and the paragraph repeats the shape until the analysis ends.

blocks.heading: Comparing throughout
blocks.text: Comparing throughout is an analysis where both texts are in view in each paragraph; two separate commentaries placed side by side compare nothing, because no sentence refers across. The test is the cover-up: hide one column of the answer, and if the visible column still makes sense, it was describing its text rather than relating the pair. The organisation by form, structure and language is available — the task names all three — and so is any other arrangement that keeps the pair in view; the structure is judged by whether the relation stays present in each paragraph.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a paragraph that compares
blocks.text: From a feature article and the diary written from it: "Both texts put the same morning in front of their readers, but the article spreads it across a frame that opens at dawn and closes at dusk, whereas the diary compresses it into the hour its writer lived — the structural choice suits each audience, since the magazine reader has chosen an arc and the diary’s page is a life’s fragment. The article’s closing image of the boy at the tank returns to its opening fog, a cyclical shape my diary never attempts, because a diary ends where the day did." Two texts in every sentence, three grounds covered, and the explanation in the purposes: the paragraph is the shape to build.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The comparison is the second task of Paper 1, and it follows the response it analyses: fifteen marks, five for reading and ten for analysis, opened by the instruction Compare. Form, structure and language need not be taken in separate sections — the task names them as grounds, not as headings — and any organisation that keeps both texts in view serves. The three habits that carry the marks: quote briefly from both texts, join every pair with a connective, and end each point with the purpose or audience the difference serves.

blocks.heading: Two texts, no bridge
blocks.text: The structural failure of comparison is discussing each text in turn without ever referring across to the other: a paragraph on the source, then a paragraph on the response, repeated, with no sentence holding both. The reader is left to do the comparing the task asked for. The fix is the paired point, built on a connective, in every paragraph — whereas, similarly, in contrast — and the check is mechanical: find the connective, or find the paragraph that needs rewriting.
